santa-marinha.name: Monastery of Santa Marinha da Costa
santa-marinha.short: A 12th-century Augustinian monastery on the slope of Penha, rebuilt in the 16th–18th centuries and now a historic pousada
santa-marinha.long: The Monastery of Santa Marinha da Costa stands on the slope of the Penha hill above Guimarães. In the 12th century it was given to the Augustinian canons, who over three and a half centuries enlarged the church and built four wings around a cloister. In 1528 a Hieronymite college was founded here, and in 1541 King John III granted it the right to award degrees. The monastery was rebuilt in the 17th and 18th centuries, a fire gutted it in 1951, and in 1972 the state bought it. The conversion into a hotel was designed by Fernando Távora, who won the National Architecture Prize of 1987 for the work.
santa-marinha.history:
The monastery stands on a site where, it is thought, a small single-nave church with an apse already existed at the end of the 9th century, itself built over a Roman settlement. Archaeologists have found traces of pre-Roman and Roman occupation. Some believe this was the site of the palaces of the counts of Portucale, with the monastery church serving as their palatine chapel.

At the end of the 11th century the site became a monastery, and in the 12th century it was handed to the regular canons of Saint Augustine. In the three hundred and fifty years they held it, the church was enlarged and four new wings were built around a new cloister. On 27 January 1528, by a bull of Pope Clement VII, the Order of Saint Jerome was established here with a college that taught the humanities and arts and then theology. In August 1537 the humanist Nicolaus Clenardus visited the college; he wrote that the prior, Frei Diogo de Murça, kept three lecturers there, one of them teaching rhetoric to "a son of the king, fourteen years old". In 1541 a charter of John III allowed the college to grant the degrees of bachelor, licentiate and doctor of arts, equal to those of Coimbra. The students included royal sons, as a plaque in the church records. In that same 16th century the monastery gained a new high altarpiece by Frei Carlos, a new cloister and a remodelled church façade.

The works of the 17th and 18th centuries changed the monastery most of all: the conventual wings were rebuilt, a new chancel was added in 1713, the interior was brought up to date, and the monastery enclosure took its present shape.

After the male religious orders were dissolved, the monks were told to leave, the building passed to the state and was then sold at auction to private owners. In 1951 a great fire destroyed much of the complex, including the azulejo panels on the walls leading to the friars' cells and the stone staircase to the chapter house. The monastery then stood utterly abandoned.

In 1972 the state bought the building, and five years later restoration work began with a view to turning it into a hotel. The project for the reconstruction and adaptation was drawn up by the architect Fernando Távora, who received the National Architecture Prize of 1987 for it. According to IPPAR, the work produced one of the most important archaeological campaigns ever carried out in a medieval building in Portugal. The garden with its box-hedge borders was also kept, running down the slope of Penha; its avenues are lined with century-old trees, a small stream feeds a round tank at the top of the garden, and at the north-west corner of the cloister there survives the base of a tower with a pre-Romanesque Mozarabic door. As early as 1936 the monastery and its church had been listed as an Imóvel de Interesse Público.

Today it is the Pousada Mosteiro Guimarães, a historic hotel in the Pousadas de Portugal network. The two-storey block holds 27 rooms, and the former cells hold a further 22 rooms and 2 suites; the D. Mafalda restaurant occupies the old monastic cellars and the bar the former kitchen. The gardens, covering about nine hectares with architectural and landscape features, are listed as being of public interest.
facts: The monastery was given to the Augustinian canons in the 12th century, and they held it for about 350 years.
A bull of Clement VII founded a Hieronymite college here in 1528; in 1541 John III gave it the right to award degrees.
In 1936 the monastery and its church were listed as an Imóvel de Interesse Público.
A fire in 1951 destroyed the azulejo panels by the monks' cells and the stone staircase, and the building lay abandoned for decades.
The conversion into a pousada was designed by Fernando Távora, who won the National Architecture Prize of 1987 for it.
santa-marinha.tip: The pousada is a working hotel, but the D. Mafalda restaurant in the old cellars and the bar in the former monastery kitchen are open to outside guests by reservation. The gardens and the church can be visited; the park runs down the slope of Penha towards the city. Driving is easiest, with free parking; you can also ride the cable car up to Penha and walk back down. Combine it with the castle and the historic centre, about ten minutes away by car.
